title: Hrithik Roshan Wanted ₹500 Crore for Krrish 4. His Father Just Called That 'Nonsense.'
excerpt: Rakesh Roshan breaks silence on the budget clash rumors, the YRF partnership, and why India's most famous superhero is 'on another planet' while his fans wait.
body:
For thirteen years, Krrish has been frozen. The cape is in the closet. The mask is gathering dust. India's first genuine superhero franchise — the one that taught an entire generation that a Bollywood hero could fly and make you believe it — has been stuck in development limbo since Krrish 3 hit theatres in 2013. And in the vacuum left by silence, gossip rushed in.

The latest rumor was a doozy: Hrithik Roshan had allegedly demanded a jaw-dropping ₹500 crore budget for Krrish 4, insisting on world-class VFX and action sequences worthy of a global superhero film. Yash Raj Films, the production partner, reportedly wanted to cap costs at ₹350 crore to keep the project commercially viable. The clash, the story went, had stalled the entire production.

This week, Rakesh Roshan — the filmmaker-father who created the franchise with Koi... Mil Gaya in 2003 — sat down with Mid-Day and, in characteristic Roshan fashion, dispatched the drama with a single word.

"It's all nonsense that Hrithik has asked for a ₹500 crore budget for top-tier VFX and world-class action for his directorial debut, while YRF wants to cap costs at ₹350 crore. Making a good film catering to a wide audience takes time. Even I have taken time for each of my Krrish offerings." — Rakesh Roshan

The Director in the Mirror

Here is what makes Krrish 4 genuinely interesting, far beyond the budget gossip: Hrithik Roshan is directing it himself. This is not a star cameo or a vanity credit. Rakesh Roshan announced in 2025 that his son would take over the director's chair, making Krrish 4 Hrithik's directorial debut — a move that is either extraordinarily brave or borderline reckless, depending on which corner of Film City you are standing in.

The franchise has been through a revolving door of filmmakers. Karan Malhotra was initially attached to direct, with Siddharth Anand on board as co-producer. Both eventually departed. Multiple scripts were reportedly developed and discarded. By the time Hrithik decided to direct it himself, the project had become less a sequel and more a test of institutional patience.

Rakesh Roshan, however, is unbothered. When asked about the delay, he offered the kind of quote only a proud father can deliver without irony: "Krrish is on another planet and we are all waiting for his dates." He is referring to the production company Hrithik launched earlier this year, which has kept the actor-turned-producer consumed with new commitments.

The Stakes Are Absurd

Consider the landscape Krrish 4 is walking into. In 2026, Bollywood budgets have ballooned to previously unthinkable levels. Dhurandhar 2 cost ₹225 crore and returned ₹1,850 crore worldwide. The YRF Spy Universe — Pathaan, War, Tiger — has normalized tentpole budgets in the ₹250-350 crore range. A ₹500 crore ask, while eye-popping, is not as outlandish as it sounds when your competition is literally Hrithik's own former franchise-mate SRK, whose Pathaan rewrote the box office rulebook.

But Krrish carries a different kind of weight. This is India's superhero. Not a spy. Not a soldier. A man in a mask who fights aliens and saves the world to a Rajesh Roshan score. The expectations are not just commercial — they are emotional. An entire diaspora grew up watching Krrish leap across buildings in theatres from Mumbai to Toronto. The film's success could significantly impact how Indian cinema is perceived abroad, influencing remittances and cultural ties as families share the experience of watching a beloved character return to the screen. The VFX cannot look like a video game cutscene. The action cannot feel like a lesser Marvel imitation. Whatever the budget lands at — ₹350 crore, ₹500 crore, or somewhere in between — the film has to look like nothing India has ever produced.

What We Know (and Don't)

Rakesh Roshan insists everything is smooth: "There are no issues; all is smooth. It's teamwork between Adi, Hrithik, and me." By "Adi," he means Aditya Chopra, YRF's notoriously private chief, whose studio is bankrolling the project.

What we do not know: when shooting begins, who the villain is, whether the film connects to the YRF Spy Universe (unlikely but never say never with Aditya Chopra), or what version of Krrish Hrithik intends to bring back. The original was an innocent, almost naive superhero — closer to Christopher Reeve's Superman than anything in the MCU. Whether Hrithik darkens the tone or preserves the earnestness will define whether Krrish 4 is a resurrection or a reimagining.

For now, the cape stays in the closet. But the Roshans want you to know: nobody is fighting. The superhero is just busy. He will return when he is ready.

And honestly? After thirteen years, what is a little more patience?
